title: What is the Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters) architecture, how does it isolate domain logic from infrastructure (dependency inversion), and why is it a style you layer on top of microservices/monolith rather than an alternative to them?
shortTitle: What is the Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters) architecture, how does it isolate domain logic from infrastructure, and why is it a style you layer on top of microservices or a monolith?
keyPoints: Domain logic sits at the center and depends on nothing external; it never imports Spring, JPA, or HTTP classes.
Ports are interfaces owned by the domain: inbound ports (use cases) and outbound ports (repositories, external clients).
Adapters are concrete implementations: REST controllers (inbound) and JPA repositories (outbound).
Dependency inversion: the domain declares interfaces; adapters implement them; dependencies point inward.
The domain can be unit-tested with in-memory fakes, zero database, zero web server.
Hexagonal is a code-organization style inside a deployable, not an alternative to microservices or a monolith.
Apply it where domain logic is rich (loan approval, settlement); keep trivial CRUD services simpler.

s1_definition.oneliner: Put the business rules in the center with technology-agnostic ports, plug concrete adapters onto those ports, and make everything depend inward so you can swap any technology without touching the domain.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Domain** – entities, value objects, and domain services holding business rules; depends on nothing external.
- **Inbound ports** – interfaces defining use cases (e.g., `ApproveLoanUseCase`); driven by adapters like REST controllers.
- **Outbound ports** – interfaces defining what the domain needs (e.g., `LoanRepository`, `CreditBureauPort`); implemented by outbound adapters.
- **Adapters** – concrete implementations: REST controller (inbound), JPA repository (outbound), HTTP client (outbound).
- **Dependency rule** – all dependencies point inward; the domain owns the interfaces; adapters depend on and implement them.
- **Not a deployment choice** – hexagonal is a code-organization style applied inside a monolith or inside each microservice.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the loan-approval department at National Bank of India as the heart of the business. Around it are standardized slots (ports): one slot accepts applications whether they come by web, mobile, or phone. Another slot sends records out whether to Oracle or PostgreSQL. The web form, the mobile app, and the Oracle connector are all adapters that plug into these slots. If the bank switches databases, you unplug one adapter and plug in another -- the loan rules in the heart are not touched.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Hexagonal Architecture

            Inbound Adapters                 Outbound Adapters
  ┌─────────────┐                           ┌─────────────────┐
  │ REST        │──┐                   ┌───►│ JPA Repository  │
  │ Controller  │  │   ┌───────────┐   │    └─────────────────┘
  └─────────────┘  ├──►│           │───┤
  ┌─────────────┐  │   │  DOMAIN   │   │    ┌─────────────────┐
  │ Kafka       │──┘   │           │   └───►│ HTTP Client     │
  │ Listener    │      │ ports =   │        │ (Credit Bureau) │
  └─────────────┘      │ interfaces│        └─────────────────┘
                       └───────────┘
                     Dependencies point INWARD
                     Domain depends on NOTHING external

  Package Structure
  com.bank/
  ├── domain/
  │   ├── model/       (entities, value objects)
  │   ├── port/        (interfaces: inbound + outbound)
  │   └── service/     (domain services)
  ├── adapter/
  │   ├── in/          (REST controller, Kafka listener)
  │   └── out/         (JPA repo, HTTP client)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Hexagonal architecture puts the business rules at the center and surrounds them with ports (interfaces) and adapters (concrete technology implementations). The dependency rule is that everything points inward: the domain depends on nothing external and never imports Spring, JPA, or HTTP classes. Inbound adapters like REST controllers drive the domain through inbound ports, and the domain reaches outward through outbound ports implemented by outbound adapters like JPA repositories.

The payoff is testability and technology independence. At National Bank of India, Pankaj could unit-test the loan approval rule with in-memory fakes, no database and no web server, and when the bank migrated its database the team only wrote a new adapter while the approval rule stayed untouched.

The key point is that hexagonal is not an alternative to microservices or a monolith. Microservices and monolith are deployment choices; hexagonal is code organization inside one unit. You apply hexagonal inside each service where the domain logic is rich, and keep trivial CRUD services simpler.

Remember one sentence: put the business rules in the center with technology-agnostic ports, plug concrete adapters onto those ports with dependencies pointing inward, and you can swap any technology by writing a new adapter without touching the domain.
